text: The hotel can _____ up to 200 guests.
note: A building or room accommodates people: it has space for them. Include and involve are about what is part of something; comprise means "consist of".

text: Many students find it difficult to _____ with the pressure of exams.
note: Cope with = deal successfully with something difficult. Handle and control take no "with": handle the pressure.

text: Sales have _____ sharply over the last two years, and the shop may have to close.
note: Decline = become less. (It can also mean say no politely: decline an invitation.) Refuse, reject and deny are only about saying no.

text: After hours of talks, the two sides finally reached a _____ that both could accept.
note: Reach a compromise = agree by each side giving up something. We make (not reach) a promise or a commitment.

text: _____ at the club's meetings has fallen since they were moved to Saturday.
note: Attendance = how many people go to something. Careful: assistance means help (Spanish asistencia can mean both).

text: He tried to _____ his disappointment, but everyone could see he was upset.
note: Conceal = hide, often a feeling or a fact. Store, keep and save are about things you put away, not feelings you hide.

text: It is _____ that you arrive on time for the interview, or they won't see you.
note: Crucial = extremely important. Severe, acute and intense describe how strong something bad is: a severe storm, acute pain.

text: The new airport is expected to _____ tourism in the region.
note: Boost = help something increase or improve. Rise and arise have no object; we heighten a feeling (heighten tension), not tourism.

text: He didn't want to become a _____ to his family when he got older.
note: Be a burden to someone = be a problem they have to take care of. Weight and load are about physical heaviness.

text: The minister refused to _____ on the rumours about her resignation.
note: Comment on something = give your opinion about it. Mention and say take no "on"; tell on someone means report their bad behaviour.

text: She had prepared well and passed the exam with _____.
note: With ease = easily, without difficulty. Comfort is about feeling physically relaxed; simplicity describes a thing, not how you do it.

text: I've decided to _____ on an evening course in Spanish.
note: Enrol on a course (British; American: enroll in). We sign up for a course, subscribe to a magazine and apply for a place.

text: The cost of the repairs could _____ £1,000.
note: Exceed = be more than an amount or limit. Overcome a problem, excel at something, overtake a car.

text: The singer rose to _____ after appearing on a TV talent show.
note: Rise to fame = become famous. A reputation is what people think of you, good or bad; you don't rise to it.

text: All our washing machines come with a two-year _____.
note: A guarantee = the maker's promise to repair or replace a product. Insurance is something you pay a company for.

text: My working hours are quite _____, so I can pick the children up from school.
note: Flexible hours = you can change when you work. Elastic and loose describe materials and clothes.

text: Under no _____ should you give your password to anyone.
note: Under no circumstances = never, in any situation (a fixed phrase, always plural). Note the word order after it: should you.

text: At only £10, this jacket is a real _____.
note: A bargain = something bought for much less than it is worth. A sale is an event; a discount is the money taken off the price.

text: Students have free _____ to the library's online resources.
note: Access to = the right or chance to use something. Entry and admission are about going into a place.

text: Please _____ attention to the safety instructions before the flight.
note: Pay attention to = listen or watch carefully. A fixed phrase: always pay.

text: Many people find it hard to _____ up smoking, even when they know it is harmful.
note: Give up = stop doing something. Take up smoking means start, which doesn't fit "even when they know it is harmful".

text: You should _____ advantage of the good weather and go for a walk.
note: Take advantage of = use a good situation. A fixed phrase: always take.

text: The concert was cancelled _____ to the heavy rain.
note: Due to = because of. We say because of (not because to), as a result of and for this reason.

text: The hotel was full, so we had no _____ but to stay at a campsite.
note: Have no choice but to = be forced to do something. A fixed phrase.

text: Studying abroad was a great _____ that taught me a lot about myself.
note: An experience = something that happens to you. An experiment is a scientific test; knowledge is uncountable (not "a knowledge").

text: He _____ me to bring an umbrella, but I forgot.
note: Remind someone to do something = tell them so they don't forget. You remember something yourself; nobody remembers you to do it.

text: The doctor _____ me to get more sleep.
note: Advise someone to do something. Suggest and recommend don't take this pattern: the doctor suggested (that) I get more sleep.

text: I'm afraid I can't _____ to go on holiday this year, because I haven't saved enough money.
note: Can afford to do something = have enough money for it. We pay for something, spend money on something, and something costs money.

text: Could you _____ an eye on my bag while I go and buy a coffee?
note: Keep an eye on = watch something so it stays safe. A fixed phrase.

text: It isn't easy to _____ a living as a freelance designer.
note: Earn a living (or make a living) = get the money you need to live. You win a prize and gain experience.

text: My parents never _____ in my decisions about what to study.
note: Interfere in = get involved in something that isn't your business. Disturb, bother and prevent take a direct object, not "in".

text: The airline agreed to _____ passengers for the five-hour delay.
note: Compensate someone for a loss or problem = give them money because of it. You repay a loan, reward good behaviour and return something you borrowed.

text: She was _____ to lend him money, because he had never paid her back before.
note: Reluctant to do something = not wanting to do it. Opposed and resistant are followed by "to + -ing" (opposed to lending); doubtful is about not being sure.

text: The manager _____ from his job after the scandal.
note: Resign from a job = leave it by choice. Quit takes no "from" (quit his job); dismissed means someone else made him go; you abandon a place or a plan.

text: She went to the bank to _____ some cash for the weekend.
note: You withdraw money from a bank account. Remove means take away, extract is used for teeth or oil, subtract is maths.

text: The government has _____ a new tax on sugary drinks.
note: Impose a tax, a fine or a rule on something. Force and oblige are followed by a person and "to" (forced people to pay); command is for orders.

text: Keeping our customers safe must be our top _____.
note: Top priority = the most important thing to deal with. A preference is something you like better; importance and urgency don't go with "our top".

text: The _____ of starting a new job abroad was both exciting and frightening.
note: The prospect of (doing) something = the thought of something that may happen. A perspective is a point of view, the outlook is the likely future in general, and expectancy is used in "life expectancy".

text: The small bakery made a _____ of £20,000 in its first year.
note: Make a profit = earn more than you spend. You don't "make a benefit" or "make an advantage", and "earnings" is plural.

text: The workers have _____ to go on strike if their pay isn't increased.
note: Threaten to do something = say you will do something unpleasant. Warn is followed by "that" or a person (warned the boss); menace and alert take an object.

text: Police _____ the man of stealing the car, but they have no proof yet.
note: Suspect someone of (doing) something. You blame someone for something; doubt and mistrust aren't followed by "of".

text: The festival will go ahead _____ of the weather.
note: Regardless of = without being affected by. Despite takes no "of" (despite the weather), although is followed by a clause, and however starts a new idea.

text: I'm not very _____ on horror films; I prefer comedies.
note: Keen on = liking something. Fond takes "of", interested takes "in", and eager is followed by "to" or "for".

text: Passengers are asked to _____ from smoking anywhere on the train.
note: Refrain from (doing) something = not do it. Avoid and stop are followed directly by -ing (avoid smoking); you prevent someone from doing something.

text: We really enjoyed the trip in _____ of the bad weather.
note: In spite of = despite. You can say "despite the bad weather" or "in spite of the bad weather", but never "in despite of".

text: Many local people _____ to the plans for a new motorway.
note: Object to something = be against it. Oppose takes no "to" (oppose the plans), you protest against something and disagree with it.

text: He became _____ to online games when he was a teenager.
note: Addicted to something. Dependent takes "on", obsessed takes "with", and keen takes "on".

text: Once you have had the illness, you are _____ to it for the rest of your life.
note: Immune to an illness = your body can't catch it again. Safe and protected take "from"; secure is not used about illness.

text: I kept looking at my watch, but he didn't take the _____ and stayed until midnight.
note: Take the hint = understand what someone is quietly trying to tell you. The other words don't go with "take the" in this meaning.

text: She breathed a _____ of relief when she heard her son was safe.
note: Breathe a sigh of relief is a fixed phrase. You can't "breathe a breath", and a puff or a blow has nothing to do with relief.

text: He's often late, but I'll give him the _____ of the doubt this time.
note: Give someone the benefit of the doubt = believe them although you aren't sure. It is a fixed phrase.

text: I'd like to _____ a complaint about the noise from the flat upstairs.
note: Make a complaint is the usual collocation. We don't say do, give or put a complaint.

text: Could you _____ me a favour and post this letter on your way to work?
note: Do someone a favour = help them. It is always "do", never make, give or take.

text: It's important to _____ a good impression at a job interview.
note: Make a good impression = cause people to think well of you.

text: My sister _____ her driving test on her third attempt.
note: Pass a test or exam. Succeed takes "in" (succeeded in passing), manage takes "to", and you achieve a goal or result.

text: He _____ far too much money on clothes and shoes.
note: Spend money on something. You pay for something, something costs money, and a shop charges you.

text: Excuse me, could you _____ me how to get to the station?
note: Tell someone how to do something. Say and explain don't take a person straight after them (explain to me how), and speak isn't used this way.

text: The film was so boring that I _____ asleep halfway through.
note: Fall asleep = start sleeping. You can "go to sleep", but not "go asleep" or "get asleep".

text: It's a long drive, so we'd better _____ off early in the morning.
note: Set off = start a journey. Put off means delay, take off is for planes, and turn off is for lights or roads.

text: Have you _____ your homework yet, or are you still watching TV?
note: Do homework is the fixed collocation. We don't make, take or perform homework.

text: It took her a long time to _____ over the shock of losing her job.
note: Get over = recover from something upsetting or an illness. The other verbs don't combine with "over" in this meaning.

text: He was _____ of stealing the money, but he insisted he was innocent.
note: Accuse someone of a crime. You blame someone for something, charge someone with it, and punish someone for it.

text: Our flight was _____ for two hours because of thick fog.
note: Delayed = happening later than planned because of a problem. Postpone is a choice to move an event to a later date; extend makes something longer.

text: The shop assistant gave me the wrong _____, so I had to go back and ask for two pounds more.
note: Change is the money you get back when you pay more than the price. Coins are single pieces of money, and exchange is swapping one thing (or currency) for another.

text: The match was called _____ because the pitch was under water.
note: Call off = cancel. Call out and call down exist, but not with this meaning, and "call away" means to ask someone to leave.

text: I can't _____ up my mind which of the two jobs to accept.
note: Make up your mind = decide. A fixed phrase; the other verbs don't go with "up my mind".

text: I'm really looking _____ to seeing you again next summer.
note: Look forward to = wait for something with pleasure. "To" is a preposition here, so it is followed by -ing: looking forward to seeing.

text: It's not worth _____ the risk of losing your job just for one afternoon off.
note: Take a risk (or take the risk of). We don't make, do or have a risk.

text: The captain _____ the blame for the defeat, although it wasn't entirely his fault.
note: Take the blame (for something) = accept that you are responsible for it. The other verbs don't go with "blame" in this way.

text: She has a great _____ of humour and can make anyone laugh.
note: A sense of humour is the fixed phrase. We use "feeling" for emotions, and "taste" for what people like (a taste for music).

text: Could you please _____ quiet? The baby is asleep.
note: Keep quiet = not make any noise. (Stay quiet is also possible, but it is not among the choices.) Hold, make and take do not go with "quiet".

text: It was such a _____ film that I couldn't sleep that night.
note: -ing adjectives describe what causes the feeling: a frightening film. -ed adjectives describe the person who feels it: I was frightened. Afraid is never used before a noun.

text: There is no point _____ about something you can't change.
note: There is no point (in) is followed by the -ing form: no point worrying, no point waiting.

text: The two companies have decided to _____ forces and share their research.
note: Join forces = work together. A fixed phrase. Connect, attach and link are about fixing things together physically or by a system.

text: She was moved to _____ by the sad ending of the book.
note: Moved to tears is the fixed phrase. We say "burst into tears" or "in tears", not "in cries".

text: The twins look so alike that I can never _____ them apart.
note: Tell two things apart = see the difference between them. Say, speak and see don't work with "apart" in this meaning.

text: Prices have gone _____ again this month, so we can't afford to eat out so often.
note: Go up = increase. Prices go up or rise; they don't go high, over or above.

text: The government has promised to _____ more money in schools and hospitals.
note: Invest money in something = use it to get a benefit later. Spend takes "on" (spend money on schools), and you pay for or buy a thing, not "in" it.

text: This museum is well worth _____, even if you only have an hour.
note: Be worth + -ing: worth visiting, worth trying, worth reading. After "worth" we never use "to" + infinitive.

text: My boss is very _____ and gets annoyed if anyone arrives even five minutes late.
note: Punctual = always on time. Accurate and exact describe facts and numbers, and regular means "happening again and again".

text: I'm trying to _____ down on sugar and fatty food.
note: Cut down on something = eat, drink or use less of it. The other verbs don't combine with "down on" in this meaning.

text: After hours of talks, the two sides managed to _____ to an agreement.
note: Come to an agreement = finally agree. You reach an agreement (no "to"), and arrive at a place, not at "an agreement to".

text: He tried to _____ his way out of trouble by telling the police a long story.
note: Talk your way out of something = escape a problem by what you say. A fixed phrase; speak, say and tell don't work here.

text: Could you _____ me a lift to the station, please?
note: Give someone a lift = take them somewhere in your car. We lend things like books or money, but not lifts.

text: It's hard to _____ a living as a freelance artist.
note: Earn a living = get enough money to live on by working. Gain, win and collect don't go with "a living".

text: The company's profits _____ by ten per cent last year.
note: Rise (rose) has no object: profits rose. Raise (raised) needs one: the company raised its prices. Arise means "begin to exist" (a problem arises).

text: Could you _____ an eye on my bag while I buy a ticket?
note: Keep an eye on something = watch it to make sure it is safe. A fixed phrase.

text: I'm sorry I _____ my promise. It won't happen again.
note: Break a promise = not do what you said you would. You keep or break a promise; you can fail to do something, but not "fail a promise".

text: Over 500 students took _____ in the competition.
note: Take part in something = join in. Take place means "happen" and never takes "in" with a person's activity.

text: The ceremony will take _____ in the main hall at noon.
note: Take place = happen (for planned events). Take part means "join in", so it needs a person doing something.

text: I'm sure he broke the window on _____; it wasn't an accident.
note: On purpose = deliberately. An aim or a goal is something you want to achieve, and we say "by accident", not "by purpose".

text: You need to book tickets well in _____ because they sell out quickly.
note: In advance = beforehand. "In front" is about position, and "ahead" can't follow "in".

text: You can stay in my room for the time _____, until you find a flat.
note: For the time being = for now, until something changes. A fixed phrase.

text: His explanation doesn't make any _____ to me.
note: Make sense = be clear and reasonable. We don't "make meaning", "make reason" or "make logic" in this way.

text: It's a complete _____ of time arguing with him; he never listens.
note: A waste of time (or money) = something that gives no useful result. A lack of time means "not enough time".

text: We've run _____ of milk, so I'll go to the shop.
note: Run out of something = have none left. Run down means "lose power", and run away means "escape".

text: I can't put _____ with this noise any longer!
note: Put up with = tolerate. A fixed phrasal verb: the particle must be "up".

text: Our car _____ down on the motorway, and we had to wait for help.
note: Break down = stop working (a car or machine). Fall down is for people or things dropping to the ground.

text: The weather _____ out to be much better than we expected.
note: Turn out (to be) = prove to be, in the end. A fixed phrase.

text: I came _____ some old photos while I was tidying the attic.
note: Come across something = find it by chance. Come over means "visit", and "come along" means "come with someone".

text: Please carry _____ with your work while I answer the phone.
note: Carry on = continue. Carry over means "move to a later time", and the others don't work here.

text: She really takes _____ her mother; they have the same laugh.
note: Take after someone = look or behave like an older relative. Take on means "accept work" and take over means "take control".

text: The new law brought _____ many changes in the way we work.
note: Bring about = cause something to happen. Bring up means "raise a child" or "mention", and bring down means "make fall".

text: Children often look _____ to their older brothers and sisters.
note: Look up to someone = respect and admire them. Look down on someone means the opposite.

text: The bad weather didn't put us _____; we went camping anyway.
note: Put someone off = make them lose interest or enthusiasm. A fixed phrasal verb.

text: Scientists have made a major _____ in the fight against cancer.
note: A breakthrough = an important new discovery or achievement. A breakdown is a failure, and a breakup is the end of a relationship.

text: It took me ages to get _____ the flu, and I missed two weeks of work.
note: Get over an illness or a shock = recover from it. The other particles don't work with "get" in this meaning.

text: After hours of arguing, he finally gave _____ and let her choose.
note: Give in = stop arguing and accept what the other person wants. Give out means "distribute" and give away means "give for free".

text: They _____ up the company in 1999 with only three employees.
note: Set up a company = start it. Put up means "build" or "raise" (put up a tent, put up prices).

text: I'll _____ you up at eight, so be ready to go.
note: Pick someone up = collect them by car. Take and bring need a destination; lift up means "raise".

text: Cheer _____! Things will get better soon.
note: Cheer up = become happier (often as an order). The other particles don't work here.

text: The police are _____ into the robbery and have questioned three people.
note: Look into something = investigate it. Watch, see and view don't combine with "into".

text: She _____ up a story to explain why she was late.
note: Make up a story or excuse = invent it. The other verbs don't combine with "up" in this meaning.

text: He's always _____ off about his new car.
note: Show off = try to impress people with what you have or can do. Boast and brag take "about" (boasting about), not "off".

text: What does the abbreviation "UN" _____ for?
note: Stand for = be short for. Mean has no "for", and say and signify aren't used like this.

text: The two friends _____ out over money and haven't spoken since.
note: Fall out (with someone) = have an argument and stop being friends. A fixed phrasal verb.

text: She _____ down the job offer because the salary was too low.
note: Turn down an offer = refuse it. Take it, and you accept; the other verbs don't work with "down" here.

text: Can anyone _____ up with a better idea?
note: Come up with an idea = think of it. Put up with means "tolerate".

text: I'm fed _____ with waiting; let's go somewhere else.
note: Be fed up (with something) = be bored or annoyed with it. A fixed phrase.

text: Most of the tickets were sold _____ within an hour.
note: Sold out = no more left to buy. Sell off means "sell cheaply to get rid of".

text: Don't worry about the test. It'll be a piece of _____.
note: A piece of cake = something very easy. A fixed phrase.

text: We only see each other once in a blue _____.
note: Once in a blue moon = very rarely. A fixed phrase.

text: I'm feeling a bit under the _____ today, so I'm staying in bed.
note: Under the weather = slightly ill. A fixed phrase.

text: She knows the whole poem by _____.
note: Learn or know something by heart = be able to say it from memory. A fixed phrase.

text: I lost _____ of time and missed the last bus.
note: Lose track of time = not notice how much time has passed. You lose count of numbers and lose touch with people.

text: Don't believe him; he's just pulling your _____.
note: Pull someone's leg = tell them something untrue as a joke. A fixed phrase.

text: Good luck with your interview! I'll keep my fingers _____.
note: Keep your fingers crossed = hope that things go well. A fixed phrase.

text: That designer coat cost an arm and a _____.
note: Cost an arm and a leg = be extremely expensive. A fixed phrase.

text: He got cold _____ just before the wedding and almost cancelled it.
note: Get cold feet = suddenly feel too nervous to do something you planned. A fixed phrase.

text: We don't always see eye to _____, but we respect each other.
note: See eye to eye = agree. A fixed phrase.

text: Her name is on the tip of my _____, but I just can't remember it.
note: On the tip of your tongue = almost remembered. A fixed phrase.

text: Losing that job was a blessing in _____; I found a much better one.
note: A blessing in disguise = something that seems bad but turns out good. A fixed phrase.

text: Don't worry, we're all in the same _____; nobody has finished the work.
note: In the same boat = in the same difficult situation. A fixed phrase.

text: The money we raised was just a drop in the _____ compared with what is needed.
note: A drop in the ocean = a very small amount compared with what is needed. A fixed phrase.

text: Please keep your address book up to _____.
note: Up to date = including the latest information. A fixed phrase.

text: To put it in a _____, we lost because we didn't practise enough.
note: In a nutshell = in as few words as possible. A fixed phrase.

text: "Good luck tonight!" "Thanks!" "Break a _____!"
note: Break a leg! = Good luck (especially to actors before a show). A fixed phrase.

text: He bit off more than he could _____ when he took on three jobs at once.
note: Bite off more than you can chew = try to do too much. A fixed phrase.

text: She works two jobs to make ends _____.
note: Make ends meet = earn just enough money to live on. A fixed phrase.

text: We paid through the _____ for those concert tickets.
note: Pay through the nose = pay far too much. A fixed phrase.

text: Don't _____ the beans about the surprise party!
note: Spill the beans = tell a secret by mistake. A fixed phrase.

text: He let the cat out of the _____ when he mentioned the wedding.
note: Let the cat out of the bag = reveal a secret by accident. A fixed phrase.

text: If you think I took your keys, you're barking up the wrong _____.
note: Bark up the wrong tree = look for something in the wrong place or blame the wrong person. A fixed phrase.

text: Moving the meeting to Monday will kill two birds with one _____.
note: Kill two birds with one stone = solve two problems with one action. A fixed phrase.

text: Don't worry about the argument; it's just a storm in a _____.
note: A storm in a teacup = a lot of fuss about something unimportant. A fixed phrase.

text: Off the top of my _____, I'd say there were about fifty people there.
note: Off the top of your head = without checking or thinking carefully. A fixed phrase.

text: He got the job because his uncle pulled some _____.
note: Pull strings = use your influence or contacts to get an advantage. A fixed phrase.

text: We shouldn't announce the results yet. That would be jumping the _____.
note: Jump the gun = do something too soon. A fixed phrase.

text: We have a lot in _____: we both love jazz and hate football.
note: Have something in common = share an interest or quality. A fixed phrase.

text: All of a _____, the lights went out and everyone screamed.
note: All of a sudden = suddenly. A fixed phrase.

text: The government must stop the disease at all _____.
note: At all costs = whatever the effort or price. A fixed phrase.

text: On the _____, I think the trip was a success, despite the rain.
note: On the whole = in general. A fixed phrase.

text: I enjoy most fruit, apples in _____.
note: In particular = especially. A fixed phrase.

text: A holiday this year is out of the _____; we simply can't afford it.
note: Out of the question = impossible. A fixed phrase.

text: Children are most at _____ from the disease.
note: At risk (of / from) = in a situation where something bad could happen. We say "in danger", not "at danger".

text: The letters were all written by _____, not typed.
note: By hand = using the hands, not a machine. A fixed phrase.

text: She won three games in a _____.
note: In a row = one after another, with no break. A fixed phrase.

text: I'd like to thank her in _____, not just by email.
note: In person = by being there yourself. A fixed phrase.

text: On _____, we get about ten emails a day, but some days there are many more.
note: On average = usually, taking all cases together. A fixed phrase.

text: It's a nice café, but it's in the middle of _____, miles from anywhere.
note: In the middle of nowhere = very far from towns and other people. A fixed phrase.

text: I've put _____ a lot of weight since Christmas.
note: Put on weight = become heavier. A fixed phrase.

text: Let's eat out for a _____ tonight; I'm tired of cooking.
note: For a change = to do something different from usual. A fixed phrase.

text: We're working to a very _____ deadline, so we can't afford any delays.
note: A tight deadline = one with very little time to spare. Narrow and thin describe width, not time.

text: We had a _____ escape; the car missed us by a few centimetres.
note: A narrow escape = a situation where you only just avoided danger. A fixed phrase.

text: The village is a long way from the road, so we went on _____.
note: On foot = walking. A fixed phrase.

text: It's easy to _____ friends at university.
note: Make friends = begin friendships. A fixed phrase.

text: Please _____ an effort to arrive on time tomorrow.
note: Make an effort = try hard. A fixed phrase.

text: They fell in _____ at first sight and married a month later.
note: Fall in love = begin to love someone. A fixed phrase.

text: There was _____ rain all weekend, so the river flooded.
note: Heavy rain = a lot of rain at once. We say strong wind or strong coffee, but not strong rain.

text: I need a _____ coffee to wake me up.
note: Strong coffee or tea = with a lot of flavour. Heavy rain, but strong coffee: the adjective depends on the noun.

text: She's one of my _____ friends; we've known each other for twenty years.
note: A close friend = someone you know very well. Near and nearby are about distance.

text: The price of houses in the city centre is very _____.
note: Prices are high or low. We don't call a price tall, big or large, though we say a large sum of money.

text: It's your turn to _____ the washing-up.
note: Do the washing-up (or the cooking, the shopping). We make a meal but do the washing-up.

text: Could you _____ a photo of us in front of the castle?
note: Take a photo. We draw a picture but take a photograph.

text: Never _____ lies to your parents; they always find out.
note: Tell a lie or tell the truth. Say, speak and talk don't take "lies" as an object in this way.

text: She _____ an important role in organising the festival.
note: Play a role (or a part) in something = be involved in it. A fixed phrase.

text: She _____ a small restaurant in the city centre.
note: Run a business = manage it. Drive is for vehicles, and you don't "take" or "hold" a restaurant.

text: It was _____ a boring film that we left halfway through.
note: Such a + adjective + noun: such a boring film. We use so before an adjective alone: the film was so boring.

text: Each twin looks _____ the other, so it's hard to tell them apart.
note: Look like someone = look similar to them. Alike is used without an object: the twins look alike.

text: I'm so tired I can _____ keep my eyes open.
note: Hardly = almost not. Hard is an adjective or adverb of effort (work hard), and nearly means "almost".

text: I haven't seen her _____, so I don't know how she is.
note: Lately = recently. Late means "after the expected time" and later means "afterwards".

text: I'm not _____ to getting up so early.
note: Be used to something = be familiar with it. After "used to" with this meaning we use a noun or -ing form.

text: My parents didn't _____ me go to the party.
note: Let someone do something (no "to"). Allow and permit need "to": allowed me to go.

text: I've lived here _____ five years.
note: For + a period of time (for five years); since + a starting point (since 2020).

text: I fell asleep _____ the film, so I missed the ending.
note: During + noun (during the film). While needs a clause with a verb: while we were watching.

text: She works _____ a nurse in a large hospital.
note: As + a job = in that role. Like means "similar to".

text: She _____ on the sofa all afternoon, watching old films.
note: Lie (lay) down = rest flat; its past is lay. Laid is the past of lay (to put something down), lied is from lie (say what is untrue), and lain needs have/had.

text: We had a lot of _____ at the party; the music was great.
note: Have fun = enjoy yourself. Funny is an adjective, so it can't follow "a lot of".

text: The bank manager refused to _____ us a loan.
note: Grant someone a loan = formally agree to give it. You can lend money, but "lend a loan" is wrong.

text: She _____ the first prize in the photography competition.
note: Win a prize or a game. You beat an opponent, and you score goals or points.

text: Can I _____ your pen for a moment? Mine has run out.
note: Borrow = take something that you will give back. Lend is the opposite: you lend your pen to me.

text: This word is almost impossible to _____ into English.
note: Translate into another language. Transform means "change completely", and transport is to carry people or goods.

text: I'll lend you the money _____ you pay me back next week.
note: Provided (that) = on condition that. Unless means "if not", and although and whereas show contrast.

text: She is very outgoing, _____ her sister is quite shy.
note: Whereas = while, in contrast. Despite needs a noun or -ing form after it.

text: _____ the traffic was terrible, we arrived on time.
note: Although + a clause (subject + verb). Despite is followed by a noun or -ing: despite the traffic.

text: He was tired; _____, he kept working until midnight.
note: Nevertheless = in spite of that. Therefore shows a result, and otherwise means "if not".

text: Hurry up, _____ we'll miss the train.
note: Otherwise = if not, or else. The other words don't give a warning about what happens if you don't act.

text: It was raining heavily; _____, we stayed at home.
note: Therefore = as a result. However and although show contrast, and despite is a preposition.

text: _____ the rain, the match went ahead as planned.
note: Despite + a noun (despite the rain). Although needs a clause with a verb.

text: There was a heavy storm; _____, all the flights were cancelled.
note: Consequently = as a result. Nevertheless shows contrast, and unless and whereas aren't used this way.

text: All restaurants must _____ with the new hygiene regulations by March.
note: Comply with a rule = do what it says. Obey, follow and respect take a direct object, with no "with": obey the regulations.

text: The company was found to be in _____ of its contract and had to pay compensation.
note: In breach of a contract, rule or law = breaking it. Fracture and crack are physical breaks; an offence is a crime (you commit an offence).

text: We made it clear from the _____ that the project would take at least two years.
note: From the outset = from the very beginning. An origin or source is where something comes from; an outbreak is the sudden start of something bad (a war, a disease).

text: Refunds are only given at the manager's _____.
note: At someone's discretion = if they decide to, using their own judgement. A fixed phrase: we say "it's the manager's decision", but not "at the manager's decision".

text: Against all the _____, the small village team won the cup.
note: Against all (the) odds = although it seemed very unlikely. A fixed phrase; the other words don't go with "against all".

text: The government's spending plans have come under close _____ from the press.
note: Come under scrutiny = be examined carefully, often critically. We pay close attention to something, but nothing "comes under attention".

text: A momentary _____ of concentration caused the driver to miss the red light.
note: A lapse of concentration (or memory) = a short time when it fails. A gap is a space between things; a fault is a mistake or defect, not a moment.

text: At the age of 80, he finally agreed to _____ control of the company to his daughter.
note: Relinquish control or power = give it up, often unwillingly. You resign from a job and retire from work; neither takes "control" as an object.

text: The _____ of the work was done by volunteers.
note: The bulk of = most of. Volume, size and weight are measurements; "the volume of work" means how much work there is, not most of it.

text: The resort _____ mainly for families with young children.
note: Cater for (American: cater to) = provide what a group of people needs. Serves and supplies take an object with no "for"; attend to means deal with.

text: She quickly built up a good _____ with her students.
note: A rapport = a friendly relationship where people understand each other. Careful: a report is a written account (Spanish reporte), and in English we'd say a good relationship, not "a good relation".

text: The concert was a _____ to the band's late singer.
note: A tribute to someone = something that shows respect and admiration for them. We say in memory of and out of respect for; praise is uncountable (not "a praise").

text: The fact that the bridge is still standing is a _____ to the skill of its builders.
note: Be a testament to = clearly show how good something is. We say proof of, a sign of, and evidence is uncountable (not "an evidence").

text: She has a very low pain _____, so she hates going to the dentist.
note: A pain threshold = the point at which you start to feel pain. Limit is close in meaning but doesn't make this compound; a border is between countries.

text: Unfortunately, the meeting _____ with my dentist's appointment, so I can't come.
note: Two events clash = they happen at the same time, so you can't go to both. Crash and collide are about vehicles hitting things.

text: There's no point _____ on past mistakes: learn from them and move on.
note: Dwell on something = keep thinking or talking about it, usually something bad. The others are about being in a place and don't take "on" like this.

text: The company is about to _____ on an ambitious expansion plan.
note: Embark on something = start something new and important. We board a plane, enter a room and launch a plan (no "on").

text: Most students _____ for the online version of the course.
note: Opt for = choose. Choose, select and prefer take the thing directly, with no "for": most students choose the online version.

text: She felt lonely because she had no one to _____ in.
note: Confide in someone = tell them your secrets or private feelings. We count on and depend on someone; share takes "with".

text: Her first novel won critical _____ and quickly became a bestseller.
note: Critical acclaim = praise from critics (win / receive critical acclaim). Applause is clapping; fame is being well known, not praise from critics.

text: The new bypass should help to _____ traffic congestion in the town centre.
note: Alleviate = make a problem or suffering less bad. Soothe and comfort are for people or pain; heal is for wounds and illnesses.

text: The new law comes into _____ on 1 January.
note: Come into force = start to apply (also come into effect). A party or politician comes into power; we put a plan into practice, not a law.

text: It goes without _____ that you should back up your files regularly.
note: It goes without saying = it is obvious. A fixed phrase: always saying.

text: When the interviewer asked about her weaknesses, she was at a _____ for words.
note: Be at a loss for words = not know what to say. A fixed phrase; we say a lack of words, not "at a lack".

text: His argument doesn't hold _____: the figures he quotes are ten years old.
note: Not hold water = not be believable when you look at it closely. An idiom; we say it doesn't make sense, not "hold sense".

text: I wasn't sure he was telling the truth, but I gave him the _____ of the doubt.
note: Give someone the benefit of the doubt = believe them, although you're not sure. A fixed phrase.

text: Online banking was still in its _____ when I opened my first account.
note: In its infancy = at a very early stage of development. Childhood and youth are only used for people this way.

text: The rule applies to all staff, without _____.
note: Without exception = every one, with none left out. A fixed phrase.

text: Something is wrong with this essay, but I can't quite _____ my finger on it.
note: Can't put your finger on something = can't say exactly what it is. An idiom: always put.

text: I didn't mean to say her name instead of yours: it was a slip of the _____.
note: A slip of the tongue = a small mistake when speaking. A fixed phrase.

text: The judge stressed that her ruling did not create a legal _____ for similar cases.
note: A precedent = an earlier decision used as a guide for later ones; set or create a legal precedent. An example or instance is just one case of something; a sample is a small part used for testing.

text: After two days of discussion, the jury returned a _____ of not guilty.
note: A jury returns or reaches a verdict (guilty or not guilty). A judgement is given by a judge, and a sentence is the punishment that follows a guilty verdict.

text: Drivers who park here without a permit are _____ to a fine of up to £100.
note: Liable to a fine, a tax or a penalty = legally having to pay it. Likely and apt are followed by a verb (likely to rain); prone to is used for bad things that happen often (prone to injury).

text: I'm _____ to agree with you, although I'd like to see the figures first.
note: I'm inclined to agree = I think I agree, but not strongly. Prone and liable are about bad things that tend to happen; we say leaning towards, not leaning to agree.

text: With its narrow streets and old wooden houses, the village is _____ of a film set.
note: Reminiscent of = making you think of something. Similar takes "to", alike comes after the things compared (they are alike), and resembling takes no preposition.

text: Some parents _____ a lot of pressure on their children to do well at school.
note: Exert pressure or influence on someone (put pressure on also works). Force, press and make don't go with pressure in this way.

text: He was dismissed on the _____ that he had repeatedly broken company rules.
note: On the grounds that / on the grounds of = for this reason, usually an official one. We say for the reason that, not on the reasons that.

text: The new parking charges have become a bone of _____ between residents and the council.
note: A bone of contention = a subject people keep arguing about. A fixed phrase: no other noun works here.

text: If you don't choose a language, the app will use English by _____.
note: By default = automatically, unless you choose something else. Standard and normal are adjectives or nouns that don't follow "by" (as standard, as normal).

text: Let's _____ with the formalities: please call me Anna.
note: Dispense with = do without something you don't need. Dispose takes "of" (dispose of rubbish); discard and omit take a direct object.

text: Last year the university _____ an honorary degree on the novelist.
note: Confer something on someone = formally give an honour or a right. Award and grant take "to" (awarded a degree to her); present takes "with" or "to".

text: The region is in the _____ of the worst drought for fifty years.
note: In the grip of = strongly affected by something bad (a drought, a crisis, fear). Hold, clasp and handle are only about holding things with your hands.

text: Traffic in the city centre ground to a _____ after the accident.
note: Grind to a halt = slowly stop completely. Also come to a halt. We don't say ground to a pause, break or rest.

text: Although years have passed, she still _____ to the hope that her son is alive.
note: Cling to a hope or belief = refuse to give it up. Grip takes a direct object; keep and attach don't go with hope in this way.

text: In the _____ of the earthquake, thousands of families had nowhere to live.
note: In the aftermath of = in the period after a bad event. We say as a consequence of or as a result of, not in the.

text: She is a scientist first and _____, and a writer second.
note: First and foremost = most importantly. A fixed phrase. Utmost means greatest (of the utmost importance); uppermost means highest.

text: The suspect was taken into _____ shortly after the robbery.
note: Take someone into custody = arrest and keep them. We say put under arrest or put in jail, not taken into.

text: He was released on _____ and must report to the police every week until the trial.
note: Released on bail = let out before a trial after money is paid as a promise to return. Bond, deposit and guarantee don't follow released on.

text: The long working hours are starting to take their _____ on her health.
note: Take a or its toll on = cause damage over time. Cost, charge and fee are about money and don't fit this phrase.

text: Any costs _____ during the business trip will be paid back by the company.
note: Incur costs, debts or a fine = become responsible for paying them. Undergo and endure go with difficult experiences; contract goes with illnesses or debts, but not costs.

text: We hadn't planned a holiday: we booked the flights on the _____ of the moment.
note: On the spur of the moment = suddenly, without planning. A fixed phrase. Compare in the heat of the moment (when angry or excited).

text: The new rules will take _____ on 1 January.
note: Take effect = start to apply (also come into force). Take action means do something; power and practice don't go with take here.

text: Ladies and gentlemen, I'd like to _____ a toast to the bride and groom.
note: Propose a toast = ask everyone to drink to someone (raise a toast also works). Offer, suggest and present don't go with toast.

text: I don't know how long the meeting will last, so let's play it by _____.
note: Play it by ear = decide what to do as things happen, without a plan. A fixed phrase (learn something by heart is different).

text: Don't worry: in the _____ of time, you'll understand why we made this decision.
note: In the fullness of time = eventually, when the time is right. A fixed phrase.

text: You can't judge a whole country on the _____ of one short visit.
note: On the strength of = because of, based on. A fixed phrase (on the basis of means the same).

text: Her latest novel is head and _____ above anything she has written before.
note: Head and shoulders above = much better than. A fixed phrase.

text: The museum will remain closed until further _____.
note: Until further notice = until you are told something different. A fixed phrase used in official announcements.

text: As a rule of _____, allow one hour of study for every hour of class.
note: A rule of thumb = a practical guide based on experience, not an exact rule. A fixed phrase.

text: The new manager was given a _____ hand to run the department as she wished.
note: Give someone a free hand = let them do things their own way. Open hand and loose hand don't have this meaning.

text: The report sheds new _____ on the causes of the financial crisis.
note: Shed light on something = help to explain it. A fixed phrase; the other nouns don't go with "shed" here.

text: Diplomats worked through the night to _____ the tension between the two countries.
note: Defuse a situation = make it less dangerous or angry (from taking the fuse out of a bomb). You disperse a crowd, dismiss an idea and dismantle a machine or a system.

text: There is a _____ contrast between the wealth of the city centre and the poverty of its suburbs.
note: A stark contrast = a very clear and striking difference. Harsh is for weather, words or treatment; rough and blunt don't go with "contrast".

text: The cases we know about are probably just the tip of the _____.
note: The tip of the iceberg = a small, visible part of a much bigger problem. Most of an iceberg is under the water.

text: The storm _____ havoc across the south coast, leaving thousands without power.
note: Wreak havoc = cause great damage or disorder. The verb wreak is used almost only with havoc (or vengeance).

text: Poor housing leads to poor health, which leads to poverty: it's a vicious _____.
note: A vicious circle = a bad situation that keeps causing itself, so it is hard to escape. A fixed phrase.

text: Once the polls had closed, the result was a foregone _____.
note: A foregone conclusion = a result that everybody expects before it happens. A fixed phrase.

text: It took him years to come to _____ with the death of his brother.
note: Come to terms with something = accept a sad or difficult fact. A fixed phrase.

text: For years the authorities turned a blind _____ to the illegal dumping of waste.
note: Turn a blind eye (to something) = pretend not to notice something wrong. A fixed phrase.

text: If the factory closes, 2,000 jobs will be at _____.
note: At stake = in a situation where something important might be lost. We say "in danger" or "under threat", but not "at danger" or "at threat".

text: Many shops went out of business in the _____ of the recession.
note: In the wake of = soon after, and often as a result of, something (the wake is the line of waves behind a ship). A fixed phrase.

text: Many companies only pay lip _____ to environmental issues without changing how they work.
note: Pay lip service = say you support something without doing anything about it. A fixed phrase.

text: Because of rising costs, the council has had to _____ back its plans for a new library.
note: Scale back = make something smaller or less ambitious. ("Cut back" works too, but only "scale" is among the choices.) Shrink and narrow don't take a plan as an object in this way.

text: You've hit the nail on the _____: that is exactly what the problem is.
note: Hit the nail on the head = say exactly what is right. A fixed phrase.

text: Bear in _____ that the shop closes early on Sundays.
note: Bear in mind = remember and consider. A fixed phrase.

text: There is no cure for the virus; the illness must simply run its _____.
note: Run its course = continue naturally until it ends. A fixed phrase.

text: New measures have been introduced to _____ the effects of the drought on farmers.
note: Mitigate = make something bad less serious. Aggravate, exacerbate and intensify all mean the opposite: make it worse.

text: Some risk is _____ in every business venture; it can never be removed completely.
note: Inherent = a permanent part of something. Innate describes qualities people are born with, and intuitive and instinctive are about feelings or reactions, not risk.

text: The evidence shows beyond a _____ of a doubt that he was at the scene of the crime.
note: Beyond a shadow of a doubt = completely certain. A fixed phrase.

text: Many people take clean water for _____ and never think about where it comes from.
note: Take something for granted = expect it will always be there and not value it. A fixed phrase.

text: The company is deeply in the _____, owing the bank millions.
note: In the red = owing money. In the black means the opposite: having money in the account. A fixed phrase.

text: New evidence has finally been brought to _____.
note: Bring something to light = make it known after it was hidden. Come to light means the same without a person doing it. A fixed phrase.

text: By delaying your answer, you run the _____ of losing the offer.
note: Run the risk of (doing) something = accept a possible bad result. A fixed phrase.

text: The team fell _____ of its target by just two points.
note: Fall short of something = not reach the level you wanted. A fixed phrase.

text: She promised to help, and then went _____ on her word.
note: Go back on your word (or a promise) = not do what you said. A fixed phrase.

text: Her talent made her stand _____ from the other candidates.
note: Stand out = be easy to notice because of being better or different.

text: He cheated in the exam and somehow got away _____ it.
note: Get away with something = avoid punishment for it. A fixed phrase.

text: The project came up _____ strong opposition from local residents.
note: Come up against something = meet a difficulty. Come up with means "think of".

text: The latest figures bear _____ what the minister said last week.
note: Bear something out = show that it is true. Bear up means "cope" and bear on means "be connected with".

text: The police have ruled _____ murder; they now think it was an accident.
note: Rule something out = decide it is not possible. A fixed phrase.

text: She struggled to hold _____ her tears at the funeral.
note: Hold back (tears, a laugh) = stop yourself from showing a feeling. Hold off means "delay".

text: A fire broke _____ in the kitchen just before midnight.
note: Break out = start suddenly (a fire, a war, a disease). Break down means "stop working".

text: It all comes _____ to money in the end.
note: Come down to something = be what finally decides it. A fixed phrase.

text: She looks _____ on people who haven't been to university.
note: Look down on someone = think you are better than them. Look up to someone means the opposite.

text: I can't go along _____ your suggestion; it's far too risky.
note: Go along with something = agree with it or accept it. A fixed phrase.

text: Can you back _____ your claim with some evidence?
note: Back something up = support it with proof. Back out means "decide not to do something".

text: Please pass _____ my thanks to your parents for the lovely dinner.
note: Pass something on = give a message or an object to another person.

text: The school decided to do away _____ uniforms altogether.
note: Do away with something = stop having it. A fixed phrase.

text: Heavy snow has cut _____ several villages from the rest of the region.
note: Cut someone or something off = separate them from others, so they can't be reached.

text: He dropped _____ of university after one year to start his own business.
note: Drop out of school or university = leave without finishing.

text: The meeting has been brought _____ to Tuesday, so please check your diaries.
note: Bring a meeting forward = move it to an earlier time. Put it back means the opposite.

text: Opposition leaders are calling _____ the minister's immediate resignation.
note: Call for something = demand it publicly.

text: Don't bank _____ getting a pay rise this year; the company is struggling.
note: Bank on something = rely on it happening. A fixed phrase.

text: The minister tried to play _____ the seriousness of the crisis.
note: Play something down = make it seem less important than it is.

text: The original proposals were watered _____ before the final vote.
note: Water something down = make it weaker or less extreme.

text: Police have promised to crack _____ on illegal parking in the city centre.
note: Crack down on something = act more strictly against it. A fixed phrase.

text: Her fear of dogs stems _____ a frightening experience as a child.
note: Stem from something = have it as its origin.

text: The debate centred _____ the future of the health service.
note: Centre on (or around) something = have it as the main subject.

text: Luck also comes into _____ in a game like this, not just skill.
note: Come into play = start to have an effect. A fixed phrase.

text: I'm still trying to get to _____ with the new software.
note: Get to grips with something = begin to understand and deal with it. Come to terms with means "accept".

text: I tried to remember her name, but I drew a _____.
note: Draw a blank = fail to remember or find anything. A fixed phrase.

text: Garlic is said to keep vampires at _____.
note: Keep something at bay = stop it from coming too close or doing harm. A fixed phrase.

text: She went to great _____ to make sure all the guests felt welcome.
note: Go to great lengths = make a very big effort. A fixed phrase.

text: I'm having second _____ about moving abroad.
note: Have second thoughts = start to doubt a decision you've made. A fixed phrase.

text: A pay rise is simply not on the _____ this year.
note: On the cards = likely to happen. A fixed phrase.

text: She followed the instructions to the _____.
note: To the letter = exactly, with no mistakes. A fixed phrase.

text: It was a case of sink or _____: either we found customers, or we closed.
note: Sink or swim = succeed by your own efforts or fail completely. A fixed phrase.

text: The plan failed, so we're back to square _____.
note: Back to square one = back at the beginning, having made no progress. A fixed phrase.

text: The design was rejected, so it's back to the drawing _____.
note: Go back to the drawing board = start planning again after a failure. A fixed phrase.

text: Our holiday plans are still up in the _____ because of the strike.
note: Up in the air = not decided yet. A fixed phrase.

text: It's a long _____, but it might just work.
note: A long shot = something with only a small chance of success. A fixed phrase.

text: I was at a loose _____ all weekend, with nothing to do.
note: At a loose end = with nothing to do. A fixed phrase.

text: That watch must have cost the _____; it's solid gold.
note: Cost the earth = be extremely expensive. A fixed phrase.

text: Tax is a political hot _____ that few politicians want to discuss.
note: A hot potato = a topic that is difficult or dangerous to deal with. A fixed phrase.

text: He buttered his boss _____ before asking for a pay rise.
note: Butter someone up = flatter them to get something. A fixed phrase.

text: He has a chip on his _____ about not having gone to university.
note: Have a chip on your shoulder = feel angry about something unfair in the past. A fixed phrase.

text: The economy has finally turned the _____ after years of decline.
note: Turn the corner = begin to get better after a difficult time. A fixed phrase.

text: The law on this is still a bit of a _____ area.
note: A grey area = a situation that isn't clearly covered by the rules. A fixed phrase.

text: Small firms are asking for a level playing _____ against the big supermarkets.
note: A level playing field = a situation where everyone has the same chances. A fixed phrase.

text: I suspect that he has a hidden _____ and wants more than he admits.
note: A hidden agenda = a secret plan behind what someone says or does. A fixed phrase.

text: It's a _____ generalisation to say that all teenagers are lazy.
note: A sweeping statement or generalisation = one that is too general to be fair.

text: Immigration is always a _____ issue at election time.
note: A thorny issue = a difficult problem with no easy answer. A fixed phrase.

text: He has a vested _____ in keeping the factory open: his family has run it for years.
note: A vested interest = a personal reason to want something to happen. A fixed phrase.

text: Fame can be a mixed _____.
note: A mixed blessing = something with both good and bad sides. A fixed phrase.

text: There is a clear double _____ here: men are praised for what women are criticised for.
note: A double standard = a rule applied more strictly to one group than to another. A fixed phrase.

text: After the check-up, the doctor gave her a clean bill of _____.
note: A clean bill of health = official confirmation that someone is healthy. A fixed phrase.

text: Finishing the whole report by Friday is a tall _____.
note: A tall order = something very difficult to do. A fixed phrase.

text: The main sticking _____ in the talks was the question of pay.
note: A sticking point = a problem that stops agreement. A fixed phrase.

text: The election was a _____ moment in the country's history.
note: A watershed moment = a turning point after which things change. A fixed phrase.

text: There's a fine _____ between confidence and arrogance.
note: A fine line between two things = a very small difference. A fixed phrase.

text: The new party is a force to be reckoned _____.
note: A force to be reckoned with = a person or group that has to be taken seriously. A fixed phrase.

text: I voted for him as the lesser of two _____.
note: The lesser of two evils = the better choice when both are bad. A fixed phrase.

text: We need to iron _____ a few small problems before the launch.
note: Iron out problems = solve them. A fixed phrase.

text: I'll touch _____ with you next week to see how the project is going.
note: Touch base = make contact briefly. A fixed phrase.

text: The news of her resignation came like a bolt from the _____.
note: A bolt from the blue = a complete surprise. A fixed phrase.

text: He ignored the writing on the _____ and was shocked when the firm closed.
note: The writing on the wall = a clear sign that something bad will happen. A fixed phrase.

text: Nobody mentioned the money, but it was the elephant in the _____.
note: The elephant in the room = an obvious problem that nobody wants to discuss. A fixed phrase.

text: Setting up a business involves a lot of red _____.
note: Red tape = official rules and paperwork that slow things down. A fixed phrase.

text: Many women feel they hit a glass _____ when they try to reach senior positions.
note: A glass ceiling = an invisible barrier to promotion. A fixed phrase.

text: The new stadium turned out to be a white _____: it cost a fortune and is hardly used.
note: A white elephant = something expensive that is useless. A fixed phrase.

text: The thief was caught red-_____ as he left the shop.
note: Caught red-handed = caught while doing something wrong. A fixed phrase.

text: There is a strict pecking _____ in the office.
note: A pecking order = the ranking of people by importance. A fixed phrase.

text: The country is suffering from a serious brain _____ as graduates move abroad.
note: Brain drain = the loss of educated people to other countries. A fixed phrase.

text: He gave up his job in the city to escape the rat _____.
note: The rat race = the tiring competition of working life. A fixed phrase.

text: She saved a small nest _____ for her retirement.
note: A nest egg = money saved for the future. A fixed phrase.

text: After the argument, she gave me the cold _____ for a week.
note: Give someone the cold shoulder = ignore them on purpose. A fixed phrase.

text: The council has given the project the green _____.
note: Give something the green light = officially allow it to start. A fixed phrase.

text: An employee decided to blow the _____ on the fraud.
note: Blow the whistle on something = tell the authorities about wrongdoing. A fixed phrase.

text: She's always willing to go the extra _____ for her clients.
note: Go the extra mile = make more effort than is expected. A fixed phrase.

text: The proof of the _____ is in the eating, so let's wait for the sales figures.
note: The proof of the pudding is in the eating = you can only judge something by trying it. A fixed phrase.

text: We spent three hours on a wild goose _____ looking for a restaurant that had closed.
note: A wild goose chase = a useless search. A fixed phrase.

text: The real _____ test of a leader is how they handle failure.
note: The acid test = a decisive test of quality. A fixed phrase.

text: I have a bone to _____ with you about the way you spoke to me.
note: Have a bone to pick with someone = have a complaint to discuss with them. A fixed phrase.

text: The new manager hit the ground _____, making changes in her first week.
note: Hit the ground running = start something with energy and no delay. A fixed phrase.

text: You have to read between the _____ to understand what he really means.
note: Read between the lines = find the hidden meaning. A fixed phrase.

text: They stayed together through thick and _____.
note: Through thick and thin = in good times and bad. A fixed phrase.

text: I decided to bite the _____ and ask my boss for help.
note: Bite the bullet = do something difficult you have been avoiding. A fixed phrase.

text: After that mistake, he is on thin _____ with his manager.
note: On thin ice = in a risky situation. A fixed phrase.

text: He'll start an argument at the drop of a _____.
note: At the drop of a hat = immediately, without hesitation. A fixed phrase.

text: We reached the station in the nick of _____ and caught the last train.
note: In the nick of time = just before it was too late. A fixed phrase.

text: The band's success was just a flash in the _____.
note: A flash in the pan = something that succeeds briefly and is then forgotten. A fixed phrase.

text: Complaining about my noise, when you play loud music all night? That's the pot calling the kettle _____.
note: The pot calling the kettle black = someone criticising another for a fault they have too. A fixed phrase.

text: People never really change; a leopard can't change its _____.
note: A leopard can't change its spots = people can't change their basic nature. A fixed phrase.

text: He seems friendly, but he's a wolf in sheep's _____.
note: A wolf in sheep's clothing = a dangerous person who seems harmless. A fixed phrase.

text: I'd leave it alone; it's best to let sleeping _____ lie.
note: Let sleeping dogs lie = don't disturb a situation that is calm. A fixed phrase.

text: The new recruit simply doesn't cut the _____.
note: Not cut the mustard = not be good enough. A fixed phrase.

text: She presented a _____ argument for changing the law.
note: A compelling argument = one so convincing that it is hard to resist.

text: There is a _____ need for new housing in the city.
note: A pressing need or problem = one that must be dealt with urgently.

text: There was a _____ error in the report that nobody had noticed.
note: A glaring error = a very obvious mistake. A fixed phrase.

text: The project cost a _____ amount of money.
note: A staggering amount = so large it is hard to believe.

text: The proposal was passed by an _____ majority.
note: An overwhelming majority = a very large majority. A fixed phrase.

text: The two countries are locked in a _____ dispute over water.
note: A bitter dispute = an angry argument that lasts a long time.

text: That's a _____ exaggeration; it wasn't nearly that bad.
note: A gross exaggeration = a very great exaggeration.

text: Thinking he'll change his mind is just _____ thinking.
note: Wishful thinking = believing something because you want it to be true. A fixed phrase.

text: Ignoring the warning was a _____ mistake.
note: A grave mistake = a very serious one.

text: The first week at work was a rude _____ for her.
note: A rude awakening = an unpleasant surprise that makes you see the truth. A fixed phrase.

text: Don't jump to _____ before you've heard the whole story.
note: Jump to conclusions = decide something too quickly, without enough facts. A fixed phrase.

text: After a long debate, the committee reached a _____.
note: Reach a consensus = come to a decision that everyone accepts.

text: Both sides had to make a _____ to reach a deal.
note: Make a concession = give up something to reach agreement.

text: The two leaders will _____ talks in Geneva next week.
note: Hold talks (or a meeting, an election). We don't keep, take or make talks.

text: The campaign aims to _____ awareness of the disease.
note: Raise awareness = make more people know about something. Rise has no object.

text: We must _____ the deadline, whatever happens.
note: Meet a deadline = finish in time. We catch a bus or a train, not a deadline.

text: The project aims to _____ cooperation between schools in different countries.
note: Foster something = help it to develop. We raise children and feed people, but "foster cooperation" is the usual phrase.

text: Constant criticism can _____ a child's confidence.
note: Undermine = make weaker, little by little. Underline means "emphasise", and underestimate means "think too little of".

text: I'd love to take you up _____ your offer of a lift.
note: Take someone up on an offer = accept it. A fixed phrase.

text: He said something he regretted in the heat of the _____.
note: In the heat of the moment = while feeling strong emotion, without thinking. A fixed phrase.

text: Since the mistake, everyone in the office has been walking on _____ around him.
note: Walk on eggshells = be very careful not to upset someone. A fixed phrase.

text: On the _____ of it, the plan seems sensible, but there may be hidden problems.
note: On the face of it = judging by how it first appears. A fixed phrase.

text: The management turned a deaf _____ to the workers' complaints.
note: Turn a deaf ear to something = refuse to listen to it. A fixed phrase.

text: The bank was forced to write _____ the loan as a loss.
note: Write something off = accept that it is lost and will not be paid back. A fixed phrase.

text: With _____, it's easy to see where we went wrong.
note: With hindsight (or in hindsight) = looking back, knowing what you know now. We say in retrospect, not "with retrospect"; foresight is the opposite, seeing what will happen.

text: They hoped to settle the dispute without _____ to the courts.
note: Recourse to = using something as a way to get help, especially legal help. Don't mix it up with resource (something useful you have).

text: Several shops in the _____ of the station were damaged in the fire.
note: In the vicinity of = near. Surroundings take no "of" this way (the station's surroundings); a town has outskirts, a station doesn't.

text: After years of planning, the project finally came to _____.
note: Come to fruition = succeed after a long time of work. Plans bear fruit (not "come to fruit").

text: Despite our worries, the wedding went off without a _____.
note: Go off without a hitch = happen with no problems at all. A fixed phrase.

text: Salary will be _____ with experience.
note: Commensurate with = right in size or amount for something. The others take "to": proportional to, equal to, corresponding to.

text: I'm not _____ to the occasional glass of wine.
note: Not averse to = quite happy to have or do something (humorous understatement). Adverse means harmful (adverse effects); reluctant and unwilling are followed by to + verb.

text: All members must _____ to the club's code of conduct.
note: Adhere to a rule = follow it exactly. Obey and follow take no "to"; we comply with a rule.

text: The ugly new car park _____ from the beauty of the old town.
note: Detract from = make something seem less good. Distract means take someone's attention away; subtract and deduct are about numbers and money.

text: A goal in the last minute _____ the title for the home team.
note: Clinch a title, deal or victory = finally win it. Don't confuse it with clench (your fists or teeth).

text: The interviews have been recorded and preserved for _____.
note: For posterity = for people in the future. Heritage, ancestry and inheritance look back to the past.

text: As a child, she put her father on a _____ and couldn't see his faults.
note: Put someone on a pedestal = admire them so much that you think they are perfect. An idiom: always pedestal.

text: They got married after a _____ romance of just six weeks.
note: A whirlwind romance = one that happens very fast. Only whirlwind is used this way (also a whirlwind tour).

text: Critics say the court's ruling will open the _____ to thousands of similar claims.
note: Open the floodgates = suddenly let a lot of something happen. An idiom.

text: She has been at the _____ of the company for twenty years.
note: At the helm = in charge (a helm steers a ship). We'd also say at the head of, but not "at the steering" or "at the rudder".

text: Relations between the two countries are at a low _____.
note: At a low ebb = in a bad state (the ebb is when the sea goes out). We say at low tide (no "a"), and not about relations.

text: Tickets for the final were well _____ impossible to get.
note: Well nigh = almost (formal or literary). A fixed phrase; we say almost impossible or nearly impossible, but not "well near".

text: Farmers struggle to _____ out a living from the poor soil.
note: Eke out a living = get just enough to live on, with difficulty. We earn a living and scrape a living, both without "out".

text: I need some time to _____ it over before I make a decision.
note: Mull something over = think about it carefully for a while. Ponder and consider take no "over"; we reflect on something.

text: In _____ to her wishes, the funeral was a private one.
note: In deference to someone's wishes = because you respect them. A fixed phrase; the others don't go with "in … to".

text: The politician complained that her comments had been taken out of _____.
note: Take something out of context = repeat only part of it, so its meaning changes. A fixed phrase.

text: The two leaders are at _____ over the issue of trade.
note: Be at loggerheads (with someone) = disagree strongly. We say at a crossroads (a point of decision), at daggers drawn and cross swords.

text: She was on _____ all week, waiting to hear whether she'd got the job.
note: On tenterhooks = nervous while waiting for news. Also on pins and needles, but never on needles alone.

text: By the time the vote was held, the result was a foregone _____.
note: A foregone conclusion = a result that is certain before it happens. A fixed phrase.

text: The deal was rescued at the eleventh _____, just before the deadline.
note: At the eleventh hour = at the last possible moment. We say at the last minute or moment, but the idiom uses eleventh hour.

text: The company pays lip _____ to equality but has no women on its board.
note: Pay lip service to = say you support something without doing anything about it. We pay attention and pay tribute, but the idiom is lip service.

text: After years of not speaking, the brothers decided to bury the _____.
note: Bury the hatchet = stop arguing and become friends again. An idiom: always hatchet.

text: She made no _____ of her dislike for her new boss.
note: Make no secret of = not try to hide something. A fixed phrase.

text: His rude remarks at the dinner were completely beyond the _____.
note: Beyond the pale = completely unacceptable. An old idiom (a pale was a fence), but today only pale is used.

text: Halfway through the year, it's time to take _____ of what we've achieved.
note: Take stock (of) = think carefully about a situation before deciding what to do. A fixed phrase.

text: The company was on the _____ of collapse when a new investor stepped in.
note: On the brink of = very close to (usually something bad). A rim is the edge of a cup or wheel, a margin is an amount or the side of a page, and a border is between countries.

text: For years the gang acted with _____, knowing the police would never touch them.
note: With impunity = without being punished. An exemption frees you from a rule or tax, an indemnity is protection against loss, and "with liberty" isn't used.

text: She has a _____ for expensive shoes that her bank balance can't really support.
note: A penchant for something = a liking for it. Tendency is followed by "to", habit by "of", and leaning by "towards".

text: Talks between the union and management have reached a complete _____.
note: Reach an impasse = get to a point where no progress is possible. You can meet or face an obstacle, but you don't "reach" a blockage, hindrance or obstacle.

text: Staff were encouraged to air their _____ at the monthly meeting.
note: Air your grievances = say openly what you feel is unfair. Sorrows and pains are feelings of sadness or hurt, and injuries are physical.

text: It took a lot of patience to _____ the frightened cat out from under the bed.
note: Coax someone/something out of a place = gently persuade them to come out. Persuade, convince and urge are followed by "to" or "that", not by a place.

text: The idea is unusual, but it should be judged on its own _____.
note: Judge something on its (own) merits = by how good it really is, not by other things. It is a fixed phrase; "worth" has no plural.

text: There was a _____ agreement that nobody would mention his first marriage.
note: A tacit agreement is understood without being said. Mute and dumb describe people who don't speak, and "keep mum" means keep a secret.

text: Fears that the new factory would pollute the river proved _____.
note: Unfounded = not based on facts. Unearthed means dug up or discovered, uprooted means pulled out of the ground, and undermined means weakened.

text: In her speech she _____ to the difficulties of the past year without going into detail.
note: Allude to something = mention it indirectly. Mention and imply take no "to" (she mentioned the difficulties), and hint takes "at".

text: It is _____ on all staff to report any safety problems immediately.
note: Be incumbent on/upon someone to do something = be their duty. Obligatory, compulsory and necessary are followed by "for", not "on".

text: I'm sorry, but dealing with complaints falls outside my _____.
note: Someone's remit = the area of work they are responsible for. Range and span are about distance or time, and a rule is an instruction.

text: The office was _____ with rumours that the company was about to be sold.
note: Rife with = full of (something bad or unwanted). Abundant and plentiful aren't followed by "with", and numerous describes a plural noun (numerous rumours).

text: After a long battle, the actor finally _____ to cancer last week.
note: Succumb to an illness = die of it, or be defeated by it. Collapse, perish and expire don't take "to" in this meaning.

text: Millions of people in the region still live in _____ poverty.
note: Abject poverty = the worst, most hopeless kind. Mere means "only", sheer means "complete" (sheer luck) and plain means simple.

text: Making bread looks difficult, but it's easy once you've got the _____ of it.
note: Get the knack of something = learn how to do it. You have a skill, talent or flair for something, but you don't "get the skill of it".

text: He only speaks a _____ of Italian, but it's enough to order a meal.
note: A smattering of a language = a little of it. A sprinkling is a little of something spread over a surface, and scattering and spattering are about throwing or splashing.

text: New evidence has cast _____ on the witness's version of events.
note: Cast doubt on something = make people less sure it is true. The other words don't go with "cast".

text: The plan was nipped in the _____ when the council refused permission.
note: Nip something in the bud = stop it at an early stage, before it grows. It is a fixed phrase.

text: It's a _____ of the times that so many young people still live with their parents.
note: A sign of the times = something typical of the period we live in. It is a fixed phrase.

text: She's got a lot on her _____ at the moment, with a new job and a baby on the way.
note: Have a lot on your plate = have a lot of work or problems to deal with.

text: The committee rejected the proposal out of _____, without even discussing it.
note: Reject something out of hand = at once, without thinking about it. "Out of place" means unsuitable and "out of turn" means at the wrong time.

text: He talks about loyalty, but when it comes to the _____, he always looks after himself.
note: When it comes to the crunch = when a difficult decision really has to be made.

text: The minister refused to be _____ on the date of the next election.
note: Be drawn on something = be persuaded to talk about it. Usually negative: "she refused to be drawn".

text: His alibi didn't _____ up to close examination by the police.
note: Stand up to examination/scrutiny = stay convincing when checked carefully.

text: Let's not split _____ about the wording: we all agree on what it means.
note: Split hairs = argue about tiny, unimportant differences.

text: The meeting starts at nine on the _____, so please don't be late.
note: At nine on the dot = at exactly nine o'clock. "On the spot" means immediately or at the place where something happens.

text: She has been working all the hours God _____ to finish the book on time.
note: Work all the hours God sends = work as much as you possibly can. It is a fixed phrase.

text: After the scandal, the bank's reputation was in _____.
note: In tatters = badly damaged or destroyed. People can be "in rags" (in old torn clothes), but a reputation is "in tatters".

text: By and _____, the conference was a success, despite a few technical problems.
note: By and large = on the whole, generally. It is a fixed phrase.
