text: After years of losing, the challengers finally _____ the tables on the champions.
note: Turn the tables (on someone) = change a situation so that you now have the advantage. A fixed phrase.

text: The question of money proved to be a major stumbling _____ in the peace talks.
note: A stumbling block = something that makes it hard to make progress. A stepping stone, by contrast, helps you progress.

text: The first results _____ well for the future of the project.
note: Bode well (or ill) = be a good (or bad) sign for the future. The verb bode is hardly ever used in any other way.

text: The detective soon realised that the letter was a red _____, meant to lead him away from the real culprit.
note: A red herring = something that distracts you from the real point. A red flag is a warning, so it doesn't fit here.

text: Their repeated pleas for help fell on deaf _____.
note: Fall on deaf ears = be ignored. A fixed phrase.

text: Years of protest finally _____ in the overthrow of the regime.
note: Culminate in = reach a final, important result after a long process. Terminate and cease mean "stop", and finalise means "complete the details".

text: In some rural areas, ancient superstitions still _____ sway over daily life.
note: Hold sway = have power or influence over a place or people. A fixed phrase.

text: Tension between the two departments finally came to a _____ last week.
note: Come to a head = reach a point where something must be dealt with. A fixed phrase.

text: She accepted two extra days off in _____ of payment for her overtime.
note: In lieu of = instead of. A formal fixed phrase. In view of means "because of", and in spite of and in the face of are about difficulties.

text: Defence spending took the lion's _____ of the budget.
note: The lion's share = the largest part of something. A fixed phrase.

text: The discovery _____ the way for a new generation of treatments.
note: Pave the way for something = make it possible or easier. A fixed phrase.

text: After years of effort, their research was at last beginning to bear _____.
note: Bear fruit = produce good results. A fixed phrase, used for plans and efforts as well as plants.

text: If we make an exception now, it may prove to be the thin end of the _____.
note: The thin end of the wedge = a small first step that leads to much bigger, usually unwelcome, changes. A fixed phrase.

text: Fame can be a double-edged _____: it brings money, but takes away your privacy.
note: A double-edged sword = something with both good and bad effects. A fixed phrase.

text: The last _____ came when he forgot her birthday for the third year in a row.
note: The last (or final) straw = the last of a series of bad things, after which you can't accept any more. A fixed phrase.

text: You should take everything he says with a pinch of _____.
note: Take something with a pinch of salt = don't completely believe it. A fixed phrase.

text: After the accident, it was touch and _____ for several days.
note: Touch and go = very uncertain, with a real risk of a bad result. A fixed phrase.

text: Winning the national title was another feather in the coach's _____.
note: A feather in your cap = an achievement to be proud of. A fixed phrase.

text: The professor spoke at great _____ about his early years in Cambridge.
note: At length = for a long time and in detail; "at great length" is the usual phrase. We say "in depth" for studying something thoroughly.

text: A large number of voters who were sitting on the _____ finally decided to back the new party.
note: Sit on the fence = refuse to choose between two sides. A fixed phrase.

text: It was a _____ victory: they won the case, but the legal costs ruined them.
note: A Pyrrhic victory = a win that costs so much it is almost a defeat (after King Pyrrhus of Greece). A fixed phrase.

text: His shyness is his Achilles' _____; it stops him applying for promotion.
note: Someone's Achilles' heel = their one weak point (from the Greek hero killed by an arrow in the heel). A fixed phrase.

text: This argument cuts both _____: it helps our case, but it helps theirs too.
note: Cut both ways = have good and bad effects, or help both sides. A fixed phrase.

text: There has been a sea _____ in public attitudes to recycling over the last decade.
note: A sea change = a big, complete change. A fixed phrase.

text: The concert was the great singer's swan _____: she retired the following year.
note: Someone's swan song = their last performance or work before leaving. A fixed phrase.

text: Ignoring the problem is like burying your head in the _____.
note: Bury your head in the sand = refuse to face an unpleasant fact. A fixed phrase.

text: Let me play devil's _____ for a moment and argue against the plan.
note: Play devil's advocate = argue against something to test it, even if you agree with it. A fixed phrase.

text: Everything he invests in turns to gold: he seems to have the Midas _____.
note: The Midas touch = the ability to make money from everything you do. A fixed phrase.

text: After losing the election, the president became a lame _____ with no real power.
note: A lame duck = a leader who is about to leave office and has little power. A fixed phrase.

text: The firework display turned out to be a damp _____.
note: A damp squib = something that fails to impress after being expected to. A fixed phrase.

text: The investigation opened up a whole can of _____.
note: Open a can of worms = start dealing with a problem that creates many other problems. A fixed phrase.

text: The top job turned out to be a poisoned _____: three managers had already failed in it.
note: A poisoned chalice = an honour that is likely to bring trouble. A fixed phrase.

text: He solved the problem by simply cutting the Gordian _____.
note: Cut the Gordian knot = solve a difficult problem in a quick, bold way. A fixed phrase.

text: Space is at a _____ in this tiny flat, so we have to be organised.
note: At a premium = very scarce, so very valuable. A fixed phrase.

text: He's in the _____ with his wife for forgetting their anniversary.
note: In the doghouse = in trouble with someone because of something you did. A fixed phrase.

text: Investing everything in a start-up was a real leap of _____.
note: A leap of faith = a decision to trust something without proof. A fixed phrase.

text: Don't rest on your _____; there is still a lot of work to do.
note: Rest on your laurels = be satisfied with past success and stop trying. A fixed phrase.

text: She burned the midnight _____ for weeks to finish her thesis.
note: Burn the midnight oil = work late into the night. A fixed phrase.

text: Losing the final in the last minute was a bitter _____ to swallow.
note: A bitter pill to swallow = something unpleasant that must be accepted. A fixed phrase.

text: His first day on the front line was a baptism of _____.
note: A baptism of fire = a very difficult first experience of something. A fixed phrase.

text: It's time to grasp the _____ and have an honest conversation with her.
note: Grasp the nettle = deal boldly with a difficult problem. A fixed phrase.

text: Employees are expected to toe the _____ and follow the company's rules.
note: Toe the line = obey the rules. A fixed phrase.

text: She decided to _____ her time and wait for the right moment to speak.
note: Bide your time = wait patiently for a good chance. A fixed phrase.

text: Don't rub salt in the _____ by reminding him of the exam he failed.
note: Rub salt in the wound = make a bad situation worse. A fixed phrase.

text: Her sarcastic comment took the wind out of his _____.
note: Take the wind out of someone's sails = make them lose confidence or enthusiasm. A fixed phrase.

text: The new teacher was thrown in at the deep _____ and had to teach on her first day.
note: Be thrown in at the deep end = have to do something difficult with no preparation. A fixed phrase.

text: This result is a far _____ from what we expected.
note: A far cry from something = very different from it. A fixed phrase.

text: After the argument, everyone gave him a wide _____.
note: Give someone a wide berth = keep away from them. (Not "birth": the word comes from a ship's berth.) A fixed phrase.

text: After the scandal, the government is on the back _____.
note: On the back foot = in a defensive position, forced to react. A fixed phrase.

text: She decided to take a back _____ and let the younger staff lead the project.
note: Take a back seat = become less involved or less important. A fixed phrase.

text: The tabloids had a field _____ with the minister's mistakes.
note: Have a field day = enjoy a chance to do something you love, often at someone's expense. A fixed phrase.

text: She's head over _____ in love with her new neighbour.
note: Head over heels (in love) = completely in love. A fixed phrase.

text: The press got _____ of the plan and published it before the announcement.
note: Get wind of something = hear about it, often a secret. A fixed phrase.

text: The sudden rain put a _____ on the celebrations.
note: Put a damper on something = spoil the enjoyment of it. A fixed phrase.

text: The mother put her foot _____ and refused to let him go to the party.
note: Put your foot down = insist firmly on something. Put your foot in it means "say something embarrassing". A fixed phrase.

text: I really put my foot in _____ when I mentioned her ex-husband.
note: Put your foot in it = say something embarrassing or tactless. A fixed phrase.

text: Residents are up in _____ about the plan to close the library.
note: Be up in arms = be angry and protesting. A fixed phrase.

text: When she asked me about it, I was at a _____ for words.
note: At a loss (for words) = not knowing what to say. A fixed phrase.

text: I'm in two _____ about whether to accept the job or stay where I am.
note: In two minds = unable to decide. A fixed phrase.

text: Many small shops went to the _____ during the recession.
note: Go to the wall = fail, especially in business. A fixed phrase.

text: The inspector went strictly by the _____ and ignored everyone's excuses.
note: Go by the book = follow the rules exactly. A fixed phrase.

text: There is nothing illegal here: the deal was entirely above _____.
note: Above board = open and honest. A fixed phrase.

text: The results were a mixed _____: some were excellent, some were poor.
note: A mixed bag = a collection of very different things or qualities. A fixed phrase.

text: Delays are par for the _____ on this railway line.
note: Par for the course = normal and expected (often something unpleasant). A fixed phrase.

text: The answer was only a shot in the _____, but it turned out to be right.
note: A shot in the dark = a guess made without any information. A fixed phrase.

text: The office has been at sixes and _____ since the move.
note: At sixes and sevens = in a state of confusion. A fixed phrase.

text: We hadn't booked, so we had to take pot _____ at the restaurant.
note: Take pot luck = accept whatever is available. A fixed phrase.

text: Their only daughter is the apple of her father's _____.
note: The apple of someone's eye = a person they love very much. A fixed phrase.

text: Once bitten, twice _____: I'll never lend him money again.
note: Once bitten, twice shy = after a bad experience you are more careful. A fixed phrase.

text: "A stitch in time saves _____," my grandmother used to say about mending things early.
note: A stitch in time saves nine = fixing a small problem now prevents a bigger one later. A fixed phrase.

text: All that glitters is not _____, so check the company's accounts first.
note: All that glitters is not gold = things that look attractive may not be valuable. A fixed phrase.

text: The grass is always greener on the other _____, but you should be happy with what you have.
note: The grass is always greener on the other side = other people's situations always look better. A fixed phrase.

text: A rolling stone gathers no _____, so she never stays in one job for long.
note: A rolling stone gathers no moss = a person who keeps moving doesn't build up a settled life. A fixed phrase.

text: Make hay while the sun _____: the offer won't last long.
note: Make hay while the sun shines = use a good opportunity while it lasts. A fixed phrase.

text: The official gave the report only a _____ glance before signing it.
note: A cursory glance = a quick look without paying attention to detail.

text: I caught only a _____ glimpse of the president as the car sped past.
note: A fleeting glimpse or moment = one that lasts a very short time.

text: A _____ doubt remained in her mind, even after the explanation.
note: A lingering doubt = one that does not go away. A fixed phrase.

text: It was an _____ struggle to win support for the new tax.
note: An uphill struggle (or battle) = a very difficult effort. A fixed phrase.

text: The discovery of penicillin ushered _____ a new era in medicine.
note: Usher in something = mark the start of it. A fixed phrase.

text: The building's design harks _____ to the 1950s.
note: Hark back to something = remind people of an earlier time. A fixed phrase.

text: The disaster galvanised the whole world into _____.
note: Galvanise someone into action = shock or excite them so that they act. A fixed phrase.

text: The report glosses _____ the real problems and focuses on small successes.
note: Gloss over something = treat it so briefly that its importance is hidden. A fixed phrase.

text: He skirted _____ the question and talked about something else.
note: Skirt around an issue = avoid dealing with it directly. A fixed phrase.

text: She pored _____ the documents until two in the morning.
note: Pore over something = study it very carefully. A fixed phrase.

text: Officers sifted _____ the wreckage for clues.
note: Sift through something = examine a large amount of material carefully. A fixed phrase.

text: He fell foul _____ the law when he failed to pay his taxes.
note: Fall foul of something = get into trouble by breaking a rule. A fixed phrase.

text: Her views on the subject are completely at odds _____ those of her colleagues.
note: At odds with = in disagreement with. A fixed phrase.

text: In a negotiation, silence can be tantamount _____ agreement.
note: Tantamount to = amounting to, equivalent to (usually something bad).

text: By the end of the evening I was bereft _____ ideas.
note: Bereft of something = completely without it. A fixed phrase.

text: A quiet, comfortable room is conducive _____ studying.
note: Conducive to something = helping it to happen.

text: He is hell-bent _____ revenge and will not listen to advice.
note: Hell-bent on something = determined to do it, whatever the cost. A fixed phrase.

text: The old town is steeped _____ history and tradition.
note: Steeped in something = full of it. A fixed phrase.

text: The apple trees were laden _____ fruit.
note: Laden with something = carrying a lot of it.

text: The plan is fraught _____ danger, and nobody should attempt it alone.
note: Fraught with something = full of (usually problems or danger).

text: The report is riddled _____ errors and should not be published.
note: Riddled with something = full of it, especially something bad.

text: He remains wedded _____ the idea that the old methods are best.
note: Be wedded to something = be so attached to it that you won't change.

text: The company's finances have been in _____ since the manager left.
note: In disarray = in a confused and disorganised state. A fixed phrase.

text: The new regulations seem to fly in the _____ of everything we have learnt about safety.
note: Fly in the face of something = go against it openly. A fixed phrase.

text: He decided to throw caution to the _____ and go ahead.
note: Throw caution to the wind(s) = take a risk without worrying. A fixed phrase.

text: The singer's comeback was greeted with _____ applause.
note: Rapturous = expressing great joy or enthusiasm. Rapt means "completely absorbed" (rapt attention), and rapture is the noun.

text: The scandal could _____ the party's chances in the next election.
note: Jeopardise = put in danger. Jettison means "throw away", jostle means "push", and juggle means "keep several things going at once".

text: The old man had a _____ look, as if he had not slept for days.
note: Haggard = looking tired, worried or ill. Haughty means "proud", haphazard means "disorganised", and hapless means "unlucky".

text: The critics _____ the new play as a masterpiece.
note: Hail something as = praise it publicly as. Haul means "pull", hammer means "hit" or "criticise", and hamper means "hinder".

text: Her speech was _____ with references to her childhood.
note: Peppered with something = containing many examples of it. Pelt means "throw things at".

text: The company has been _____ by a series of financial scandals.
note: Beset by problems = continually troubled by them. Bereaved is for someone whose relative has died, and belittled means "made to seem unimportant".

text: The minister was accused of trying to _____ the issue with vague promises.
note: Obfuscate = make something less clear on purpose. Obliterate means "destroy completely", and ostracise means "exclude from a group".

text: The report painted a _____ picture of life in the city: crime, poverty and decay.
note: A bleak picture = depressing, with no hope. Bland means "dull", blunt means "direct", and blatant means "obvious" (used for bad things).

text: Their relationship was _____ by constant arguments about money.
note: Marred by something = spoilt by it. Marketed means "advertised and sold".

text: The board was _____ to take drastic action after the figures were published.
note: Compelled to do something = forced to. Complied means "obeyed" (complied with), and compiled means "put together".

text: The talks _____ on the question of who would control the oil revenue.
note: Founder = fail, especially after a problem. Flourish means the opposite: succeed.

text: She has an _____ memory and can recall every detail of what happened.
note: Uncanny = strange and surprising, as if from a mysterious source. Unctuous means "insincerely friendly", and uncouth means "rude".

text: The charity relies on the _____ of private donors.
note: Munificence = great generosity. Magnificence is splendour, and malevolence is the wish to harm.

text: There's a storm _____ in the party over who should be the next leader.
note: A storm is brewing = trouble is developing. A fixed phrase.

text: His remarks about the budget ruffled a few _____ at head office.
note: Ruffle someone's feathers = annoy or upset them. A fixed phrase.

text: Don't rock the _____; everything is going well at the moment.
note: Rock the boat = cause trouble in a stable situation. A fixed phrase.

text: I'm happy to help, but I draw the _____ at lying for you.
note: Draw the line at something = refuse to go further than a certain point. A fixed phrase.

text: The organisers pulled out all the _____ to make the opening ceremony unforgettable.
note: Pull out all the stops = make the greatest possible effort (from the stops of an organ). A fixed phrase.

text: I'm spread too _____ at the moment, with three projects running at once.
note: Be spread thin = have too many things to do to do any of them well. A fixed phrase.

text: He kept a low _____ after the scandal and refused all interviews.
note: Keep a low profile = avoid attracting attention. A fixed phrase.

text: The threat of sanctions raised the _____ in the negotiations.
note: Raise the stakes = increase what can be won or lost. A fixed phrase.

text: She kept going off at a _____ during the lecture and never reached her point.
note: Go off at a tangent = suddenly start talking or thinking about something different. A fixed phrase.

text: I'll be there on time, come hell or high _____.
note: Come hell or high water = whatever difficulties there are. A fixed phrase.

text: Most of my new year's resolutions fell by the _____ before February.
note: Fall by the wayside = fail or be abandoned before the end. A fixed phrase.

text: After the crash, his life was hanging by a _____ for days.
note: Hang by a thread = be in a very uncertain and dangerous state. A fixed phrase.

text: The detectives left no _____ unturned in their search for the missing girl.
note: Leave no stone unturned = try every possible way. A fixed phrase.

text: The company hit rock _____ in 2009, when it nearly went bankrupt.
note: Hit rock bottom = reach the worst possible state. A fixed phrase.

text: By the age of thirty he was mortgaged to the _____.
note: To the hilt = completely, as much as possible (the hilt is the handle of a sword). A fixed phrase.

text: She passed her driving test by the skin of her _____.
note: By the skin of your teeth = only just. A fixed phrase.

text: His book is a _____ work in the field of linguistics, still quoted fifty years later.
note: A seminal work = one that strongly influences later work. A fixed phrase.

text: The new drug has undergone _____ testing over several years.
note: Rigorous = very careful and thorough. Rigid means "stiff" or "not flexible".

text: The professor has long _____ the cause of animal rights.
note: Espouse a cause or belief = support it publicly.

text: Such policies only _____ resentment among the workers.
note: Engender = cause a feeling or situation to exist. Enrage means "make very angry" and cannot take "resentment" as its object.

text: Fast-food outlets have _____ in recent years, and there are now six on our street.
note: Proliferate = increase quickly in number.

text: Interest in the project has begun to _____ since the original funding ran out.
note: Wane = gradually become weaker or smaller. Wax is the opposite, but it is used mainly for the moon.

text: The storm showed no sign of _____, and the roads remained closed.
note: Abate = become less strong. Abet means "help someone do wrong" and abolish means "officially end".

text: The inquiry _____ him of any blame for the accident.
note: Exonerate = officially say that someone is not guilty. Exacerbate means "make worse".

text: The Court of Appeal _____ his conviction, and he walked free.
note: Quash a decision or conviction = officially cancel it.

text: The company _____ its offer when it discovered the true state of his finances.
note: Rescind = officially cancel an agreement or decision.

text: The government's aim is to _____ poverty within a generation.
note: Eradicate = destroy completely. Evacuate means "move people out of danger".

text: He is friendly in public, but in private he keeps everyone at arm's _____.
note: Keep someone at arm's length = avoid getting too close to them. A fixed phrase.
